abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is characterized by pathological alpha-synuclein (-syn) accumulation and alterations in autophagy. While biological sex is increasingly recognized as a modifier of PD susceptibility and pathophysiology, its relationship with striatal autophagic-lysosomal alterations remains incompletely understood. In this study, we investigated sex-dependent changes in related molecular markers in a mouse model overexpressing -syn. Male and female C57BL/6J mice received bilateral intranigral injections of adeno-associated viral vectors encoding mutant A53T -syn or empty vectors. Dorsal striatal tissue from 29 animals was analyzed at 60 or 120 days post-injection. Confocal imaging of LC3B (microtubule-associated protein 1 light chain 3 beta; autophagosome marker) and LAMP1 (lysosomal-associated membrane protein 1; lysosomal marker) immunofluorescence quantified marker-positive areas, puncta densities, and colocalization. Associations with -syn immunoreactivity, striatal dopaminergic innervation, and axonopathy severity were also examined. At 60 days, no vector-related differences in autophagic-lysosomal markers were detected. However, at 120 days, vector x sex interactions were identified for LC3-positive area, LAMP1-positive area, and LC3 puncta density. Post-hoc comparisons showed reductions in all three measures in -syn males relative to male controls, whereas the corresponding comparisons in females were not significant. After adjustment for striatal -syn immunoreactivity, -syn males had lower LC3- and LAMP1-positive areas, LC3-LAMP1 colocalization area, and LAMP1 puncta density than -syn females. Across -syn mice, greater LAMP1 puncta density was associated with more advanced axonopathy after adjustment for sex and time. These findings identify sex-dependent alterations in striatal autophagic-lysosomal markers following A53T -syn overexpression and suggest an association between lysosomal organization and axonopathy severity. They also underscore the importance of considering biological sex in studies of PD pathophysiology and when evaluating therapies targeting protein clearance pathways.
